# Rotavirus infection

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Rotavirus infection*

[Original Article Link](/library/IL0Y_g)

---

## Summary

<u>Rotaviruses</u> are a common cause of <u>viral gastroenteritis</u> in <u>infants</u> and young children and are transmitted via the fecal-oral route. After a short <u>incubation period</u> of one to three days, patients present with symptoms of variable severity, which may include <u>vomiting</u>, <u>watery diarrhea</u>, high-grade <u>fever</u>, and <u>malaise</u>. Most patients with <u>rotavirus</u> infection receive a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> of acute <u>viral gastroenteritis</u>; diagnostic studies are usually not necessary, as they do not alter management. For patients with severe disease or in whom the diagnosis is uncertain, <u>rotavirus</u> infection can be confirmed by <u>antigen</u> detection in the stool. Treatment is supportive and mainly involves <u>fluid replacement</u> and managing symptoms as needed. <u>Rotavirus</u> infection can be prevented by <u>vaccination</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* A major cause of severe <u>diarrhea</u> in <u>infants</u> and children in the US (especially during the winter)  [[1]](/library/LI1wWR0)

* Leading cause of severe <u>diarrhea</u> among <u>infants</u> and children worldwide, although all age groups are susceptible to infection.

* Most commonly occurs in daycare centers and kindergartens




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Rotavirus</u> is a nonenveloped, segmented, double-stranded <u>RNA</u> <u>reovirus</u>.

* Transmission: fecal-oral route (e.g., by contact with hands, objects, food, water contaminated with the <u>virus</u>)





![Rotavirus](media/te301t3srpkmigxgpgz59320.jpg)

Rotavirus




References:[[2]](/library/RSalzP)[[3]](/library/5eYizL)

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Mucosal</u> damage and villous <u>atrophy</u> in the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u> impair absorption of <u>sodium</u> and loss of <u>potassium</u> → nonbloody, <u>watery diarrhea</u>

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Incubation period</u>: 1–3 days

* <u>Fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* <u>Vomiting</u> and <u>watery diarrhea</u>

* Can be severe: > 10 loose, watery stools within 24 hours

* Usually lasts 3–7 days

* Mild to severe <u>dehydration</u>: See <u>clinical signs of significant dehydration</u>.





References:[[4]](/library/3SaSzP)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)




* Diagnosis is usually clinical.

* Young children: variable presentation, ranging from no symptoms to severe disease  [[1]](/library/LI1wWR0)[[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)

* Older children and adults: usually asymptomatic or mild symptoms  [[1]](/library/LI1wWR0)[[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)

* Consider diagnostic studies for:

* Patients with <u>red flags for diarrhea</u>

* Admitted patients if <u>cohorting</u> is being considered

* Exclusion of alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>bacterial gastroenteritis</u>) [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)[[6]](/library/I0cYha0)





### Confirmatory stool studies [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)




* <u>Antigen</u> detection: via <u>enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay</u> (<u>ELISA</u>) or <u>immunochromatography</u>  [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)

* <u>PCR</u>





### Additional studies [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)[[6]](/library/I0cYha0)




* <u>Signs of significant dehydration</u>: Order <u>diagnostic studies for dehydration</u>.

* If the diagnosis is uncertain: Order <u>diagnostic studies for infectious gastroenteritis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Although a stool sample analysis can be used for diagnostic confirmation of <u>rotavirus</u> infection, management remains the same. [[7]](/library/vI1AeR0)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Norovirus infection</u>

* <u>Bacterial gastroenteritis</u>

* <u>Food poisoning</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

* Treatment is supportive (e.g., <u>fluid replacement</u>, <u>electrolyte repletion</u>, <u>antiemetics</u>). [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)[[6]](/library/I0cYha0)[[8]](/library/xMYEIp)

* Children: See “<u>Treatment of infectious gastroenteritis in children</u>.”

* Adults: See “<u>Supportive therapy for gastroenteritis</u>.”

* Patients with <u>severe gastroenteritis</u> or <u>signs of significant dehydration</u> may require inpatient treatment, including <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u>. [[6]](/library/I0cYha0)[[8]](/library/xMYEIp)[[9]](/library/J7Ys5q)

* <u>Nitazoxanide</u> may reduce the duration of illness, but evidence supporting its use is limited.  [[10]](/library/Ij1YbS0)

* For outpatients, educate patients and/or caregivers on:

* The expected duration of illness

* <u>Return precautions</u>

* <u>Prevention of rotavirus transmission</u>





> [!TIP]
> Most children with <u>gastroenteritis</u> can be safely managed at home. [[6]](/library/I0cYha0)[[11]](/library/MybMfw)

---

## Prevention

### General measures [[5]](/library/OQcIwX0)[[6]](/library/I0cYha0)[[12]](/library/Ef18LT0)




* Encourage <u>breastfeeding</u>; <u>exclusive breastfeeding</u> reduces the risk of <u>rotavirus</u> infection in young <u>infants</u>. [[6]](/library/I0cYha0)

* Offer <u>rotavirus vaccination</u> to eligible <u>infants</u>.  [[6]](/library/I0cYha0)

* Educate patients and/or caregivers on <u>preventing onward transmission of gastroenteritis</u>.

* Isolate at home until symptoms are resolved; defined in children as frequency within 2 stools/day of normal and: [[12]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* If toilet trained: no longer having accidents

* If in diapers: stool is contained within the diaper





> [!TIP]
> <u>Exclusive breastfeeding</u> during the first months of life reduces the risk of <u>rotavirus</u> infection in young <u>infants</u>. [[6]](/library/I0cYha0)




### Rotavirus vaccination [[1]](/library/LI1wWR0)[[13]](/library/nI17WR0)




* General characteristics [[1]](/library/LI1wWR0)[[13]](/library/nI17WR0)

* Live attenuated oral <u>vaccine</u>

* Two versions are available: RV1 (monovalent) and RV5 (pentavalent)

* Indications: recommended for all <u>infants</u> unless there is a contraindication [[13]](/library/nI17WR0)[[14]](/library/rSafa4)

* Contraindications to rotavirus vaccination [[13]](/library/nI17WR0)[[14]](/library/rSafa4)

* <u>Severe combined immunodeficiency</u> (<u>SCID</u>)

* History of <u>intussusception</u>: <u>Rotavirus vaccine</u> is associated with <u>intussusception</u>.

* Other general <u>contraindications for vaccination</u> (e.g., <u>allergy</u>)

* Discuss with a specialist if children: [[12]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* Are <u>immunocompromised</u> (excluding <u>HIV</u>)  [[12]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* Have preexisting chronic intestinal conditions

* Are otherwise unwell at the recommended time of <u>vaccination</u>

* Schedule: See “<u>ACIP immunization schedule</u>” for details on routine and catch-up schedules.

* Additional considerations

* The risk of <u>intussusception</u> after <u>vaccination</u> is increased in older <u>infants</u>.

* Do not start an <u>immunization</u> series in a child aged ≥ 15 weeks. [[13]](/library/nI17WR0)[[15]](/library/aWaQPj)

* No doses should be given after 8 months 0 days of age. [[13]](/library/nI17WR0)[[15]](/library/aWaQPj)

* Transient viral shedding in the stool occurs for up to 4 weeks after <u>vaccination</u>; advise strict <u>hand hygiene</u> during this period for caregivers.  [[12]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[16]](/library/8Q1OBg0)





> [!TIP]
> Children who are <u>HIV</u>-positive can safely receive the <u>rotavirus vaccination</u>, regardless of <u>CD4 count</u>. [[12]](/library/Ef18LT0)




> [!WARNING]
> Older <u>infants</u> have a higher risk of <u>intussusception</u> following <u>rotavirus vaccination</u>; to reduce this risk, do not start the <u>immunization</u> series in <u>infants</u> > 15 weeks of age and ensure the series is completed by 8 months of age. [[13]](/library/nI17WR0)[[15]](/library/aWaQPj)[[17]](/library/8s1O9R0)
